newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire opposition seek recognition by new rulers.
newsitem.headline: Zaire opposition seek recognition by new rulers.

text.p: Zaire's radical opposition demanded recognition by victorious guerrillas on Tuesday ahead of the arrival of self-proclaimed president Laurent Kabila.
Scores of supporters of opposition chief Etienne Tshisekedi chanted his name by his residence where Kabila's envoys were expected for talks on forming a new government.
Kabila's envoys had yet to meet Tshisekedi, apparently due to the opposition leader's insistence that they come to his house in Kinshasa's Limete district, opposition sources said.
The emissaries wanted the talks held in their hotel.
Kabila's rebel forces captured Kinshasa on Saturday, completing a stunning seven-month guerrilla sweep across a country the size of Western Europe.
"The (rebel) alliance forces came into Kinshasa easily because of the people. Now they must not disappoint them," said a Tshisekedi supporter in the group by his home.
Veteran dictator Mobutu Sese Seseko fled the country after the rebels took over and Kabila declared himself head of state, changing the country's name to Democratic Republic of Congo.

Kabila's senior aides have been holding consultations in Kinshasa since Monday on forming a broad-based government as urged by foreign powers. A planeload of his associates, including potential ministers, arrived in Kinshasa on Tuesday.
After a day of confusion over his travel plan, a senior aide said Kabila himself was due in the capital later on Tuesday.
Tshisekedi commands a fanatical following in Kinshasa's sprawling townships, the bastions of civilian opposition to Mobutu's 32-year dictatorship.
Mobutu sacked Tshisekedi twice as prime minister -- the last time in March this year -- but his followers maintain he is the legitimate head of government.
"Kabila must first recognise Tshisekedi as prime minister. It will be dangerous for them to try and exclude Tshisekedi," another militant said.
Opposition newspaper le Phare captured the mood in Tshisekedi's camp in its headline announcing Kabila's expected arrival in Kinshasa on Tuesday.
"Welcome Mr President, but Kinshasa has not signed a blank cheque," it wrote.
Another opposition newspaper published its version of Kabila's cabinet with Tshisekedi as prime minister, 20 posts going to Kabila's alliance and six to Tshisekedi's UDPS.
Opposition sources said a U.S. embassy official had visited Tshisekedi's residence on Monday to try to smooth the way for a meeting with Kabila's representatives.

The United States and South Africa mediated in the Zaire war. Washington voiced conditional recognition of Kabila's Congo and the rule of his Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo (AFDL), linking this to good government.
Opposition sources said the Kabila and Tshisekedi camps had consulted by telephone but it was not clear at what level.
A close adviser of Tshisekedi said they were expecting a meeting with Kabila's envoys but that he did not know precisely when. He said the "prime minister" was ready to receive them.
Tshisekedi has made no public appearances since the rebels entered town. He has generally maintained a low profile since he was last sacked by Mobutu in March.

Aides said his shadow cabinet was holding an emergency meeting under a shaded terrace in his garden where they have gathered every week since he was first removed as prime minister more than four years ago.
